docs.title: 12. Version 7 - PAM multi-view / multi-page web application
12. Version 7 - PAM multi-view / multi-page web application
docs.text:
Here we return to the initial architecture where the [métier] layer was simulated. We now know that this can be easily replaced by the actual [métier] layer. The simulated [métier] layer facilitates testing.

A JSF application is of the MVC type (Model-View-Controller):

  1. the [Faces Servlet] servlet is the generic controller provided by JSF. This controller is extended by application-specific event handlers. The event handlers encountered so far were methods of the classes serving as templates for the JSF pages
  2. The JSF pages send responses to the client browser. These are the application views.
  3. The JSF pages contain dynamic elements known as the page template. Note that for some authors, the model encompasses the entities manipulated by the application, such as the FeuilleSalaire or Employee classes. To distinguish between these two models, we can refer to the application model and the JSF page model.

In the JSF architecture, navigating from a JSFi page to a JSFj page can be problematic.

  1. The JSFi page has been displayed. From this page, the user triggers a POST via some event [1]
  2. in JSF, this POST will generally be handled by a C method of the Mi model of the page JSFi. We can say that the C method is a secondary controller.
  3. If, at the end of this method, the page JSFj needs to be displayed, controller C must:
  • update [2c], the Mj template of page JSFj
  • return [2a] to the main controller, the key for navigation that will enable the display of page JSFj

Step 1 requires that the Mi template for page JSFi reference the Mj template for page JSFj. This complicates matters somewhat, making the Mi templates dependent on one another. Indeed, the C manager for the Mi template that updates the Mj template must be aware of the latter. If the Mj template needs to be changed, the C handler for the Mi template will also need to be changed.

There is one case where model dependencies can be avoided: when there is a single M model used by all JSF pages. This architecture is only usable in applications with just a few views, but it is very simple to use. This is the one we are currently using.

In this context, the application architecture is as follows:

docs.title: 12.2.4. The [métier] layer
docs.text:
The simulated [métier] layer is modified as follows:


package metier;
 
...
public class Metier implements ImetierLocal, Serializable {
 
  // list of employees
  private Map<String,Employe> hashEmployes=new HashMap<String,Employe>();
  private List<Employe> listEmployes;
 
  // get your payslip
  public FeuilleSalaire calculerFeuilleSalaire(String SS,
    double nbHeuresTravaillées, int nbJoursTravaillés) {
    // we get the employee
    Employe e=hashEmployes.get(SS);
    // an exception is thrown if the employee does not exist
    if(e==null){
      throw new PamException(String.format("L'employé de n° SS [%s] n'existe pas",SS),1);
    }
    // a fictitious payslip is returned
    return new FeuilleSalaire(e,new Cotisation(3.49,6.15,9.39,7.88),e.getIndemnite(),new ElementsSalaire(100,100,100,100,100));
  }
 
  // list of employees
  public List<Employe> findAllEmployes() {
    if(listEmployes==null){
      // create a list of three employees
      listEmployes=new ArrayList<Employe>();
      listEmployes.add(new Employe("254104940426058","Jouveinal","Marie","5 rue des oiseaux","St Corentin","49203",new Indemnite(2,2.1,2.1,3.1,15)));
      listEmployes.add(new Employe("260124402111742","Laverti","Justine","La brûlerie","St Marcel","49014",new Indemnite(1,1.93,2,3,12)));
      // employee dictionary
      for(Employe e:listEmployes){
        hashEmployes.put(e.getSS(),e);
      }
      // we add an employee who doesn't exist in the dictionary
      listEmployes.add(new Employe("X","Y","Z","La brûlerie","St Marcel","49014",new Indemnite(1,1.93,2,3,12)));
    }
    // we return the list of employees
    return listEmployes;
  }
}
  1. line 8: the list of employees
  2. Line 7: The same list in the form of a dictionary indexed by the employee ID SS
  3. Lines 24–39: The findAllEmployes method, which returns the list of employees. This method creates a hard-coded list and references it via the employees field in line 8.
  4. Lines 27–33: A list and a dictionary of two employees are created
  5. Line 35: An employee is added to the employees list (line 8) but not to the hashEmployes dictionary (line 7). This is done so that the employee appears in the employee combo box but is not recognized by the calculerFeuilleSalaire method (line 14), causing it to throw an exception (line 17).
  6. lines 11–21: the calculerFeuilleSalaire method
  7. line 14: the employee is searched for in the dictionary hashEmployes using their ID SS. If not found, an exception is thrown (lines 16–18). Thus, we will have an exception for the employee with ID SS X added on line 35 to the employee list but not to the hashEmployes dictionary.
  8. On line 20, a dummy pay slip is created and returned.

The ApplicationData bean will have application scope:


package web.beans.application;
 
import java.io.Serializable;
import java.util.logging.Logger;
import javax.annotation.PostConstruct;
import javax.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped;
import javax.inject.Named;
import metier.IMetierLocal;
import metier.Metier;
 
@Named
@ApplicationScoped
public class ApplicationData implements Serializable {
 
  // business layer
  private IMetierLocal metier = new Metier();
  // logger
  private boolean logsEnabled = true;
  private final Logger logger = Logger.getLogger("pam");
 
  public ApplicationData() {
  }
 
  @PostConstruct
  public void init() {
    // log
    if (isLogsEnabled()) {
      logger.info("ApplicationData");
    }
  }
 
  // getters and setters
...
}
  • Line 11: The @Named annotation makes the class a managed bean. Note that, unlike in the previous project, we did not use the @ManagedBean annotation. The reason is that a reference to this class must be injected into another class using the @Inject annotation, and @Inject only injects classes with the @Named annotation.
  • Line 12: The @ApplicationScoped annotation makes the class an application-scoped object. Note that the class of the annotation is [javax.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped] (line 6) and not [javax.faces.bean.ApplicationScoped] as in the beans of the previous project.

The ApplicationData bean serves two purposes:

  • line 16: maintains a reference to the [métier] layer,
  • lines 18–19: define a logger that can be used by other beans to log to the Glassfish console.

Lines 39–44: the init method is executed after instantiation of the class (@PostConstruct). Here, it is used only to log its execution. We must be able to verify that it is executed only once per user since the class is session-scoped. Line 42: the method uses the logger defined in the ApplicationData class. This is why we needed to inject a reference to this bean (lines 18–19).

docs.title: 12.5.3. Error Handling
docs.text:
We want to be able to properly handle exceptions that may occur during the calculation of a simulation. To do this, the code for the [faireSimulation] method will use a try/catch block:


  // menu action
  public String faireSimulation(){
    try{
      // we calculate the payslip
      feuilleSalaire= ...
      // simulation is displayed
      ...
      // update the menu
      ...
       // render the simulation view
      return "simulation";
    }catch(Throwable th){
      // clear the list of previous errors
      ...
      // create a new error list
      ...
      // view vueErreur is displayed
      ...
      // update the menu
      ...
       // the error view is displayed
      return "erreurs";
    }
}

The list of errors created on line 15 is as follows:


  // the view model
  ...
  private List<Erreur> erreurs=new ArrayList<Erreur>();
...

The Error class is defined as follows:


package web.entities;
 
public class Erreur {
 
  public Erreur() {
  }
 
  // field
  private String classe;
  private String message;

  // manufacturer
  public Erreur(String classe, String message){
    this.setClasse(classe);
    this.message=message;
  }
 
  // getters and setters
...  
}

Errors will be exceptions whose class name is stored in the class field and whose message is stored in the message field.

The list of errors constructed in the [faireSimulation] method consists of:

  • the initial exception th of type Throwable that occurred,
  • its cause th.getCause() if it has one,
  • the cause of the cause h.getCause().getCause() if it exists.
  • ...

    <script type="text/javascript">

Lines 4–6 change the posted values. Note that

  1. the posted values are valid, c.a.d. they will pass the validation tests for the input fields heuresTravaillees and joursTravailles.
  2. the "raz" function does not submit the form. In fact, the form will be submitted via the link cmdEffacerSimulation. This post will occur after the "raz" function (Javascript) has been executed.

During the execution of post, the posted values will follow the normal flow: validation, then assignment to the model fields. These are as follows in the [Form] class:


  // the view model

private List<Simulation> simulations=new ArrayList<Simulation>();

The Simulation class is as follows:


package web.entities;
 
import metier.FeuilleSalaire;
 
public class Simulation {
 
  public Simulation() {
  }
 
  // simulation fields
  private Integer num;
  private FeuilleSalaire feuilleSalaire;
  private String heuresTravaillées;
  private String joursTravaillés;
 
  // manufacturer
  public Simulation(Integer num,String heuresTravaillées, String joursTravaillés, FeuilleSalaire feuilleSalaire){
    this.setNum(num);
    this.setFeuilleSalaire(feuilleSalaire);
    this.setHeuresTravaillées(heuresTravaillées);
    this.setJoursTravaillés(joursTravaillés);
  }
 
  public double getIndemnites(){
    return feuilleSalaire.getElementsSalaire().getIndemnitesEntretien()+ feuilleSalaire.getElementsSalaire().getIndemnitesRepas();
  }
 
  // getters and setters
...
}

This class allows you to save a simulation created by the user:

  • line 11: the simulation number,
  • line 12: the payslip that was calculated,
  • line 13: the number of hours worked,
  • line 14: the number of days worked.

Here is an example of a record:

The simulation number is incremented with each new record. It belongs to the SessionData bean:


  // simulations
  private List<Simulation> simulations = new ArrayList<Simulation>();
  private int numDerniereSimulation = 0;
private Simulation simulation;

The [enregistrerSimulation] method can proceed as follows:

  • retrieve the number of the last simulation from the [SessionData] bean and increment it,
  • add the new simulation to the list of simulations maintained by the [SessionData] class,

Let’s examine one of the table columns and see how it is constructed:

The code JSF for the Name column is as follows:


            <h:column>

                <h:outputText value="#{msg['simulations.headers.nom']}"/>

  1. lines 2-4: the <f:facet name="header"> tag defines the column header
  2. line 5: the employee's name is written:
    1. simulation refers to the var attribute of the <h:dataTable ...> tag: 

<h:dataTable value="#{sessionData.simulations}" var="simulation" ...>

simulation refers to the current simulation in the list of simulations: first the 1st, then the 2nd, …

  • (continued)
    1. simulation.feuilleSalaire refers to the feuilleSalaire field of the current simulation
    2. simulation.feuilleSalaire.employe refers to the employee field of the feuilleSalaire field
    3. simulation.feuilleSalaire.employe.nom refers to the "name" field of the "employee" field

The same technique is repeated for all columns in the table. There is an issue with the Indemnities column, which is generated using the following code:


            <h:column>
              <f:facet name="header">
                <h:outputText value="#{msg['simulations.headers.indemnites']}"/>
              </f:facet>
              <h:outputText value="#{simulation.indemnites}"/>
</h:column>

Line 5 displays the value of simulation.indemnites. However, the Simulation class does not have a field named indemnites. It is important to note here that the field indemnites is not used directly but via the method simulation.getIndemnites(). Therefore, it is sufficient for this method to exist. The field indemnites, on the other hand, may not exist. The method getIndemnites must return the total of the employee’s allowances. This requires an intermediate calculation because this total is not directly available in the pay slip. The method getIndemnites is provided in Section 12.5.5.

docs.title: 12.5.9. The [terminerSession] action
docs.text:
The code JSF for the link [Terminer la session] is as follows:


<h:commandLink id="cmdTerminerSession" immediate="true" value="#{msg['form.menu.terminerSession']}" action="#{form.terminerSession}" rendered="#{sessionData.menuTerminerSessionIsRendered}"/>

The action [terminerSession] associated with the link allows the user to log out and return to the empty data entry form:

If the user had a list of simulations, it is cleared. Additionally, the simulation numbering resets to 1.

docs.title: 13. Version 8: Porting the application to a Spring/Tomcat environment
13. Version 8: Porting the application to a Spring/Tomcat environment
docs.text:
Question: Following the example "Sample Application – 02: rdvmedecins-jsf2-spring" from [ref3], port the previous application to a Spring/Tomcat/Hibernate environment.

The new web application is [mv-pam-jsf2-spring-multipages]. The web interface remains unchanged:

Here is one possible approach:

  1. create a Maven project of type [Java Application] named [mv-pam-spring-metier],
  2. add the necessary dependencies,
  3. copy the elements from the previous EJB project into the new Spring project,
  4. correct any errors that appear in the Spring project,
  5. create the [persistence.xml] file that configures the JPA layer,
  6. create the Spring configuration file. At this point, the [mv-pam-spring-metier] project should be correct. Imagine a JUnit test that proves this,
  7. create a Maven project of type [Web Application],
  8. add the necessary dependencies (JSF and the [métier] layer),
  9. copy the elements of the JSF / EJB project from the previous version into the new JSF / Spring project,
  10. correct any errors that appear,
  11. copy the Spring configuration file from the [mv-pam-spring-metier] project into the web project,
  12. add the code to instantiate the Spring beans to the [ApplicationData] bean,
  13. complete the configuration file [faces-config.xml],
  14. Test the web application.
